chunks: What is wave soldering. The question: What is wave soldering?
Wave soldering is a fast way to solder many through-hole joints at once.
Parts are pushed through holes from the top, then the board's underside glides across a flowing wave of molten solder.
The solder climbs up into each hole and around each leg, and then it cools into joints. It is cheap and quick for boards with lots of through-hole parts.
Imagine sliding a flat tray across the top of a small, steady waterfall so only its underside touches the water.
Water also rises up into any narrow straw in the tray, because it is pulled up thin spaces.
Wave soldering works like this: the board's underside touches the solder wave, and solder is drawn up the holes around the legs.
One catch: the whole underside gets wet, so anything stuck on the bottom must survive that.
Side view. The board travels over the wave with its underside riding on the crest, so the protruding leads are immersed.
Through-hole leads (grey) protrude below the board; a glued SMD part (orange) sits on the bottom and is dragged through the wave, which is why it must be glued and wave-compatible.
Solder wave: a pump-fed standing ripple of molten solder, around 250 degrees Celsius for common lead-free alloys.
Flux: a cleaning agent sprayed on first so the solder sticks to clean metal. Preheat: warming the board before the wave, to activate the flux and avoid shocking the board.
Capillary action: the pull that draws liquid up a narrow gap, here up the hole. Bridging: unwanted solder joining two neighboring pins.
Through-hole part: a part with legs through drilled holes.
Say the board's contact length along the wave is 40 mm and the conveyor moves at 1. 2 m/min, which is 0. 02 m/s. Each point on the board then touches the solder for 0. 04 / 0.
02 = 2. 0 seconds. In that short time, flux has cleaned the metal, the solder rises up the holes, and the board moves off to cool. A slower belt gives longer contact.
That is the whole idea.
"Wave soldering solders through-hole boards in bulk.
The board's underside is fluxed, preheated, and then passes over a standing wave of molten solder, around 250 degrees Celsius for lead-free, for a few seconds.
Capillary action fills the holes and forms the joints.
Bottom-side SMT parts have to be glued and wave-compatible, and designs need spacing, orientation and thermal reliefs to avoid bridging and poor hole fill.
Few through-hole parts or SMT on both sides usually mean selective soldering instead."
